analysis.one_liner: Creates a national health insurance program covering doctor, dental, hospital, and nursing care, paid for with a new 5% business tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in two House subcommittees for two years and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a government-run health insurance system run through the states: everyone who met basic wage-history rules (and their dependents) could get medical, dental, hospital, home-nursing, and other care from providers of their choice, with the government paying providers directly. It would be funded by a new 5% value-added tax on business transactions, with food, rent and home purchases, and medical care exempted. People already on Medicare would use the new plan only for services Medicare doesn't cover. Benefits were to start October 1, 1992.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people who meet modest wage-history thresholds, their dependents, retirees, and the needy (covered through public agency reimbursements) would receive doctor, dental, hospital, home-nursing, and auxiliary care without premiums, deductibles, or medical bills. Medicare beneficiaries would get coverage for services Medicare doesn't pay for, and a study would be launched toward folding Medicare into the new program.

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible individual would be entitled to medical, dental, podiatric, home-nursing, hospital, and auxiliary services, choosing their own physician, dentist, or hospital [S2][S3].
The new 5% value-added tax would be zero-rated for retail food, principal-residence housing, and medical care, shielding basic necessities [S2][S3].
Provider payment rules preserve fee-for-service and patient choice, and allow physicians to keep their own practices rather than becoming government employees [S3].
Benefits would first be available October 1, 1992, with the fund financed solely by the new tax [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses would collect a new 5% tax on the sale of goods and services, which sellers generally pass on to consumers in higher prices. Private health insurers would lose much of the market for covering the newly insured population, and hospitals would face Board-set maximum payment rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers via the new tax; private insurers

drawbacks.text: Eligibility is tied to wage earnings, so people with little or no work history are covered only if a public agency reimburses the fund for their care — the bill is social insurance for workers first, not universal coverage on day one [S3].

Hospital benefits are capped at 60 days per benefit year (exclud mental-disease hospitalization), and the Board may limit dental, home-nursing, and auxiliary services when funds, personnel, or facilities fall short [S3].

A 5% value-added tax is a broad-based consumption tax; even with food, housing, and medical care zero-rated, it raises prices on most other purchases, which weighs more heavily on lower-income households [S2][S3].

The bill creates a large new administrative apparatus — a National Health Insurance Board, state plans, and local committees — whose costs and effectiveness were never tested, and it only commissions a study of how Medicare would eventually be folded in rather than resolving it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and direct: guaranteed doctor, dental, and hospital coverage for most working people and their families, eliminating out-of-pocket medical bills and covering Medicare gaps. The costs are real — a broad new tax that reaches consumers through prices, eligibility that leaves the jobless dependent on public reimbursements, and a 60-day hospital limit — but the bill was written to blunt the sharpest objections (food, housing, and medical care are tax-free; doctors keep private practices and fee-for-service). The design is dated and the financing untested, but on paper the benefit to ordinary households outweighs the cost. It never got far enough for any of this to be legislated or amended.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, where it sat for two years without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 3, 1991, and referred jointly to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees [S5][S1].
In February 1991 it was referred to the health subcommittees of both committees; that was the last action ever taken [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5][S1].
The bill had only five cosponsors, all Democrats, in a chamber where 267 of 435 members were Democrats [S4][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers kept the market intact, and businesses avoided a new 5% transaction tax. Americans without adequate coverage gained nothing; the question was left to later Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and businesses facing the new tax

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and with no roll-call votes ever taken the partisan shape rests on sponsorship alone.

industries.note: A public plan paying providers directly would displace the private insurance market for most working-age coverage; insurers could act only as agents or contracted organizations under state agreements. Insurers' interest in preserving the premium-based system ran against households' interest in coverage without premiums or bills.

Hospitals would gain a guaranteed payer for eligible patients, paid reasonable costs, but the Board could impose maximum rates and payments would default to the least expensive multi-bed accommodations. Hospitals would also stop billing insured patients directly for covered services.

Providers would keep private practices, fee-for-service options, and the right to accept or reject patients, with payment rates set regionally — but rates would be set through agreements with state agencies rather than by market bargaining.

A 5% tax would apply to most sales of property and services, with sellers liable for collection and compliance; most of this cost would be passed to consumers through prices, funding the coverage that households receive in return.
